entry: Fictional anthropomorphic teddy bear created by English author A. A. Milne and illustrator E. H. Shepard. Pooh first appeared by name in a children's story commissioned by London's *Evening News* for Christmas Eve 1925. The first book, *Winnie-the-Pooh*, appeared in 1926, followed by *The House at Pooh Corner* (1928). In 1961, [[The Walt Disney Company]] licensed film and other rights from Milne's estate, and its adaptations became one of the company's most successful franchises. Alexander Lenard's [[Latin]] translation, *Winnie ille Pu* (1958), became the only Latin book ever featured on the [[The New York Times|New York Times]] Best Seller list. The original works entered the [[Public domain|public domain]] in the United States in 2022. The character's image has faced censorship in [[China]] since around 2013, after [[Internet meme|internet memes]] likened President [[Xi Jinping]] to Pooh.

Capital and largest city of [[Manitoba]], Canada (pop., 2021: 749,607), at the confluence of the Red and Assiniboine rivers. The city is named after nearby [[Lake Winnipeg]], from Western Cree words for "muddy water." French traders built Fort Rouge on the site in 1738, and Selkirk settlers founded a settlement in 1812. The city was incorporated in 1873. Known as the "Gateway to the West," it is a railway and transportation hub. Winnipeg was the first Canadian host of the Pan American Games, in 1967. Average January highs are around −11 °C (12 °F), Its professional [[Ice hockey|ice hockey]] team is the Winnipeg Jets.

American actress. Having come to attention in the late 1980s playing "quirky" characters, she achieved success in the 1990s with dramatic roles. Her films include *Beetlejuice* (1988), *Heathers* (1989), *Edward Scissorhands* (1990) and *Bram Stoker's Dracula* (1992). She received two [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] nominations, for *The Age of Innocence* (1993) and *Little Women* (1994). After a 2001 shoplifting arrest, she took a break from acting. Her role as Joyce Byers in the [[Netflix]] series *Stranger Things* (2016–2025) brought a career resurgence and a Golden Globe nomination. Her later work includes the [[HBO]] miniseries *The Plot Against America* (2020).

American cartoonist and animator, best known for the comic strip *Little Nemo in Slumberland*. The strip, which debuted in 1905, was drawn in an [[Art Nouveau]] style and showed his mastery of color and [[Perspective (graphical)|linear perspective]]. He also produced editorial cartoons and performed chalk talks on the [[Vaudeville]] circuit. Between 1911 and 1921 he self-financed and animated ten films, including *Gertie the Dinosaur* (1914), an act in which he appeared to give orders to a trained dinosaur. His most ambitious film, *The Sinking of the Lusitania* (1918), took McCay and his assistants twenty-two months. He pioneered inbetweening, registration marks and cycling, techniques that became standard. Newspaper magnate [[William Randolph Hearst]], his employer from 1911, expected him to devote his energies to editorial illustrations, which curtailed his animation work.

British statesman and writer, prime minister in 1940–1945 and 1951–1955. He was a member of the [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative Party]] for most of his career and of the Liberal Party from 1904 to 1924. As First Lord of the Admiralty in the First World War, he oversaw the failed naval attack on the [[Dardanelles]], a prelude to the [[Gallipoli campaign]]. In the 1930s he called for rearmament to counter militarism in [[Nazi Germany]]. He became prime minister in May 1940, succeeding [[Neville Chamberlain]], and led Britain in the war against the [[Axis powers]]. Later he warned of an [[Iron Curtain|iron curtain]] of Soviet influence in Europe. He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1953. Critics have cited his imperialism, his comments on race and wartime decisions such as area bombing. Historians rank him among the greatest British prime ministers.

Major international multi-sport event for sports practiced on snow and ice, held once every four years. Sports include [[Alpine skiing|alpine skiing]], [[Biathlon|biathlon]], [[Figure skating|figure skating]], [[Ice hockey|ice hockey]] and [[Speed skating|speed skating]]. The first Games were held in 1924 at Chamonix, France. Until 1992 the Winter and [[Summer Olympic Games|Summer Games]] took place in the same year; since 1994 they have alternated on separate four-year cycles. The Games have been hosted by thirteen countries, all in the [[Northern Hemisphere]]. The United States is the only country to have won a gold medal at every Winter Games. Norway holds the record for most gold medals at a single Games, with 18 in 2026, and leads the all-time medal table.

War between the [[Soviet Union]] and [[Finland]], 1939–1940. The Soviets invaded Finland on 30 November 1939, three months after the start of [[World War II]]. Finland repelled Soviet attacks for more than two months, inflicting heavy losses. The Soviets then broke Finnish defenses on the Karelian Isthmus. The Moscow Peace Treaty, signed on 13 March 1940, ceded 9% of Finnish territory. The [[League of Nations]] deemed the attack illegal and expelled the Soviet Union. Finland kept its sovereignty, and the poor performance of the [[Red Army]] encouraged [[Adolf Hitler]] to believe an attack on the Soviet Union would succeed.

Coldest and darkest season of the year in temperate and polar climates, between [[Autumn|autumn]] and [[Spring (season)|spring]]. Winter occurs when a hemisphere is tilted away from the [[Sun]] because of the [[Axial tilt|tilt of Earth's axis]]. When it is winter in the [[Northern Hemisphere]], it is summer in the Southern Hemisphere. Winter typically brings precipitation that is mainly rain or snow, depending on climate. The shortest day and longest night fall at the [[Winter solstice|winter solstice]]. The severity of winter varies with elevation, exposure to marine winds and precipitation. [[Winnipeg]], on the landlocked Great Plains, has a January high of −11.3 °C (11.7 °F), while [[Vancouver]], on Canada's Pacific coast, has a January low of 1.4 °C (34.5 °F). Meteorologists define winter as the three calendar months with the lowest average temperatures.

Astronomical event when either pole of [[Earth]] reaches its maximum tilt away from the [[Sun]]. It is the shortest day and longest night of the year in its hemisphere, when the Sun is at its lowest arc in the sky. The date is December 21 or 22 in the Northern Hemisphere and June 20 or 21 in the Southern. Daylight hours then begin to increase again. Since prehistory, many cultures have marked the solstice with festivals and rites. Neolithic sites such as [[Stonehenge]] in [[England]] and Newgrange in [[Ireland]] are aligned with the solstice sunrise or sunset.

Flexible, usually round bar of [[Metal|metal]], commonly formed by drawing the metal through a hole in a die. Wire bears mechanical loads, often as wire rope, and carries electrical signals as [[Electrical cable|electrical cable]]. It may be square, hexagonal or flattened, as in high-efficiency voice coils in [[Loudspeaker|loudspeakers]]. Common materials include [[Copper|copper]] for conductivity and [[Steel|steel]] for strength. Wire decorated jewelry in antiquity; strip drawing was in use in [[Egypt]] by the 2nd Dynasty (c. 2890–c. 2686 BCE). Drawing replaced strip twisting in the Old World between about the 8th and 10th centuries CE. The first wire mill in [[Great Britain]] was established at Tintern in about 1568.

U.S. state in the Upper Midwest (pop., 2024: 5,960,975), bordered by [[Lake Michigan]] and [[Lake Superior]]. [[Milwaukee]] is the largest city and Madison the capital. Admitted to the Union in 1848, Wisconsin is known as "America's Dairyland" and is famous for its [[Cheese|cheese]]. Manufacturing dominates the economy, alongside [[Agriculture|agriculture]] and tourism. The state has one [[UNESCO]] World Heritage Site, comprising two buildings by [[Frank Lloyd Wright]]. The [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]] was founded in Wisconsin in 1854. Since 2016 the state has been considered a swing state in national and statewide elections.

Combination of "wit and virtue," in psychologists' definition: the ability to apply expert tacit and experiential knowledge to complex questions of life and attain a common good. Wisdom is viewed both as a stable personality trait and as a context-bound process. Throughout history it has been regarded as a key virtue in religion and philosophy. The Biblical wisdom tradition contrasted human knowledge with divine omniscience, and in [[Mahayana]] Buddhism *prajna* (insight) is wedded to compassion. [[Plato]] distinguished *sophia*, philosophical wisdom, from *phronesis*, practical wisdom, and *episteme*, scientific knowledge. Psychologists have studied wisdom since the late 1970s, building on the developmental theories of [[Erik Erikson]] and [[Jean Piaget]].

Ninth studio album by the English rock band [[Pink Floyd]], released on 12 September 1975 by Harvest Records in the [[United Kingdom]] and, a day later, by [[Columbia Records]] in the [[United States]]. Most of the album is "Shine On You Crazy Diamond," a nine-part tribute to Syd Barrett, a band co-founder who had left seven years earlier. Initial reviews were mixed, but it has since been acclaimed as one of the greatest albums of the 1970s. [[Rolling Stone]] ranked it number 264 in its 2020 list of the 500 greatest albums. By 2004 it had sold an estimated 13 million copies worldwide.

Use of magic by a person called a witch, traditionally to inflict supernatural harm or misfortune on others. Although the idea of witchcraft is largely imaginary, it has served many cultures as an explanation for evil. Belief in witchcraft as malevolent magic is attested in ancient [[Mesopotamia]], and in Europe it traces back to [[Classical antiquity]]. In medieval and early modern Europe, accused witches were usually women, and accusations often came from neighbors amid social tensions. Witch trials in early modern Europe led to tens of thousands of executions. European belief gradually dwindled during and after the [[Age of Enlightenment]]. Since the 1930s, some modern pagans have embraced the term "witch."

Person who gives testimonial evidence, orally or in writing, of what they know or claim to know. In law, a witness may testify voluntarily or under compulsion, typically at a [[Trial|trial]] or before a [[Court|court]], a grand jury or an administrative tribunal. A subpoena, issued by a [[Judge|judge]], a lawyer or a government agency, commands a person to appear. In many jurisdictions witnesses must take an oath or affirm that they will testify truthfully under penalty of perjury. A witness differs from a confidential informant, whose identity is withheld from at least one party. Outside court, witnesses also attest to the authenticity of documents, such as signatures on contracts or wills.

Ukrainian former professional boxer and heavyweight champion. He won the super-heavyweight gold medal at the 1996 Olympics and turned professional that year. Known for power and footwork unusual for his size, he held multiple heavyweight world titles from 2000 to 2015, including unified titles. With his brother Vitali he dominated the division from 2004 to 2015, a period known as the "Klitschko Era." He holds the record for the longest time spent as world heavyweight champion, at 4,382 days. In 2011 the brothers entered [[Guinness World Records]] for the most world heavyweight title fight wins.

Nigerian writer, playwright and poet. Born in Aké, Abeokuta, he was educated at [[Ibadan|Government College, Ibadan]] and later studied at the [[Leeds|University of Leeds]]. He won the 1986 Nobel Prize in Literature for his "wide cultural perspective and poetic overtones fashioning the drama of existence." He has written three novels, 25 plays and five memoirs, along with poetry collections and short stories. His play *The Invention* (1957) was produced at the Royal Court Theatre in [[London]]. Other plays include *The Lion and the Jewel* (1959) and *Death and the King's Horseman*, and his novel *The Interpreters* (1965) is among his widely read works. Many of his novels and plays are set in Nigeria, reflecting its history, culture and political struggles.

Canine native to [[Eurasia]] and [[North America]] and the largest wild member of the family [[Canidae]]. More than thirty subspecies have been recognized, including the [[Dog|dog]] and the [[Dingo|dingo]]. Wolves are the most specialized members of their genus for cooperative hunting of large prey, and they travel in family packs of a mated pair and their offspring. Wolves are territorial, and fights over territory are a leading cause of death. As an [[Apex predator|apex predator]], the wolf feeds on large hooved mammals, livestock and carrion. The global wild population is estimated at 300,000. Most recorded attacks on people have been attributed to animals with [[Rabies|rabies]].

Rare class of [[Star|star]] with unusual spectra showing broad emission lines of ionized helium and highly ionized nitrogen or carbon. Classic Wolf–Rayet stars are evolved, massive stars that have lost their outer hydrogen and are fusing helium or heavier elements in the core. Their surface temperatures range from 20,000 K to around 210,000 K, hotter than almost all other stars. They are highly luminous, though not especially bright visually because most of their output is [[Ultraviolet|ultraviolet]]. Strong stellar winds drive their mass loss. A separate group are the central stars of [[Planetary nebula|planetary nebulae]], which have shed their atmospheres to reveal a bare carbon-oxygen core.

Member of the [[Spider|spider]] family Lycosidae, named for the robust and agile hunting skills of its members. Wolf spiders live mostly alone, usually do not spin webs, and pounce on prey or chase it over short distances. They are found on every continent except Antarctica. Two of their eight eyes are large and prominent, which distinguishes them from nursery web spiders. Females carry their egg sacs attached to their spinnerets. Bites cause localized pain and swelling similar to a bee sting, but wolf spiders pose no significant medical threat to humans.

Austrian theoretical physicist and pioneer of [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]]. Nominated by [[Albert Einstein]], he received the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physics "for the discovery of the Exclusion Principle, also called the Pauli Principle," a discovery involving spin theory. To preserve energy conservation in [[Beta decay|beta decay]], he proposed in 1930 a small neutral particle, dubbed the [[Neutrino|neutrino]]; neutrinos were first detected in 1956. He also contributed to work on atomic spectra and quantum electrodynamics. He spent most of his career as a professor at [[ETH Zurich]]. Pauli also corresponded with the psychologist [[Carl Jung]] on synchronicity, and his sharp critiques earned him the nickname "the conscience of physics."

Largest land-dwelling member of the family [[Mustelidae]], a muscular and solitary [[Carnivore|carnivore]]. The wolverine (*Gulo gulo*) has a reputation for ferocity out of proportion to its size and can kill prey many times larger than itself. It is found mainly in remote northern boreal forests and tundra of the [[Northern Hemisphere]], with the greatest numbers in northern Canada, [[Alaska]] and the [[Nordic countries]], and has become essentially absent from the southern end of its range. Males weigh 11–18 kg and females about 7–10 kg. Its diet consists mainly of carrion and small mammals, and it caches food in snow or burrows. Its population has declined since the 19th century because of trapping, range reduction and habitat fragmentation.

Marvel Comics superhero and member of the [[X-Men]], first seen in *The Incredible Hulk* #180 (1974). Wolverine is the alias of James "Logan" Howlett, a mutant born in Canada in the late 19th century. He has healing abilities, a long lifespan and retractable claws. His skeleton was bonded with fictional adamantium after he became a test subject in the Weapon X program. A gruff loner prone to "berserker rages," he is among the most popular Marvel characters. [[Hugh Jackman]] has portrayed him in ten films.

Sex position in which a woman is on top of her partner. The most common variant is the cowgirl position, in which the man lies on his back and the woman straddles him, facing him or away from him. It is often cited as one of the most popular positions, especially by women, because it gives them control over the pace and depth of penetration and stimulation of the [[Clitoris|clitoris]]. The woman is usually the active partner and may also stimulate the man's [[Scrotum|scrotum]]. The position is discussed in the [[Kama Sutra]].

Short-legged, muscular [[Marsupial|marsupial]] of the family Vombatidae, native to [[Australia]]. Living species are about 1 m (40 in) long and weigh 20–35 kg (44–77 lb). Wombats are [[Herbivore|herbivores]] that eat grasses, [[Herb|herbs]], [[Bark (botany)|bark]] and [[Root|roots]]. They inhabit forested, mountainous and heathland areas of southern and eastern Australia, including [[Tasmania]], as well as an isolated patch of about 300 ha (740 acres) in central [[Queensland]].
